this chapter doesn't discuss whether God or the soul exists. It discusses whether belief in an exclusively human soul justifies causing suffering to other beings, and shows that religious traditions themselves usually answer no.
"Animals don't have souls, so there's no problem killing them."
In its most elaborate theological form, inspired by Thomism:
A being's full moral value comes from having a rational, immortal soul, created by God.
Only humans have a rational, immortal soul.
So only humans have full moral value.
Beings without full moral value were entrusted by God to human use.
So using animals for food and other purposes is permitted.

Some people believe only humans have souls, others believe animals do too, and every family can talk about this. But there's one thing everyone can see: when a dog gets hurt, it feels pain, and when it's left alone, it can get sad. To know whether it's wrong to hurt someone, we don't need to know whether they have a soul. It's enough to know they feel. And almost all religions teach us to take good care of animals.
No one can prove who has a soul and who doesn't, so that can't be the criterion for deciding whom we may make suffer. The word "animal" itself comes from the Latin

, meaning soul. And religions usually condemn cruelty: the Catechism of the Catholic Church says "it is contrary to human dignity to cause animals to suffer or die needlessly". Finally, if an animal has no afterlife, this life is all it has, which makes taking it even more serious.
"If only the soul matters, why does your own religion condemn cruelty to animals?"

text.bold: 1. The premise can't be examined by everyone (P1 and P2).

paragraph.text: Who has an immortal soul is a matter of faith, not shared evidence, and traditions disagree among themselves. In Jainism and strands of Hinduism, all living beings have a spiritual principle; in Buddhism, rebirth crosses species. Choosing one specific theology's answer to authorize harm to others is special pleading. This isn't an attack on faith: it's the demand that a criterion used to justify suffering be accessible to those who don't share the same belief.

text.bold: 2. Even in traditions that affirm a uniquely human soul, cruelty is condemned.

paragraph.text: The table in (c) shows that Christianity, Judaism, Islam, Hinduism and Buddhism have explicit teachings against making animals suffer. Those who use A17 usually attribute to religion a license it doesn't grant.

text.bold: 3. Immortality isn't what makes pain bad.

paragraph.text: Pain is bad while it's felt, here and now. Having or not having an afterlife doesn't change what an animal feels in confinement or at slaughter. There's even reason to think the opposite: if there's no compensation after death, this life is the only one the animal has, and the harm of taking or ruining it is final. C. S. (d) The strongest counter-reply: human dignity and religious permission

The most solid version doesn't say animals don't matter. It says humans have a unique dignity, grounded in the rational soul and the image of God, and that God permitted the use of animals, provided there's no cruelty. On this reading, eating meat would be compatible with faith, and veganism would demand more than religion does.

text.bold: The permission's own limit condemns current practice.

paragraph.text: The permission comes with the condition of not causing unnecessary suffering. When there are food alternatives and the dominant system involves confinement, mutilation and slaughter on an industrial scale, most of that suffering is unnecessary by the tradition's own standard.
In the Abrahamic traditions, humans receive animals as stewards caring on another's behalf, not as absolute owners.
itself rejects absolute domination. There's even a strand of Christian theology that defends animals on the basis of faith (Linzey, 1994).
Even if religion permits eating meat, none requires it. Choosing not to cause suffering remains available within all these traditions.

It's possible to believe only humans have immortal souls and, at the same time, recognize that animal suffering matters. There's no contradiction between the two beliefs; the contradiction lies in condemning cruelty while funding it when it can be avoided.

The argument expresses an intuition that deserves respect: that there's something special about human life and that we have a responsibility no other animal has. For billions of people, this intuition is lived through faith, and an honest book needn't attack it. It's also true that the ultimate nature of consciousness remains an open question in philosophy and science: no one can fully explain why subjective experience exists.

But none of these points leads to the conclusion that we may make animals suffer needlessly. The special responsibility traditions attribute to humans is, in almost all of them, a responsibility to care. And uncertainty about the nature of consciousness doesn't erase the evidence that animals feel.
